```text
/**
 * Superseded worker-stream ranges.
 *
 * "Retry from here" and "edit in place" rewind a conversation to an earlier
 * message: the messages after it are deleted and the message is re-delivered,
 * either to a fresh worker or to the same worker on a resumed ACP session. The
 * worker stream is append-only, so everything the abandoned attempt produced —
 * including the original copy of the re-delivered user message — stays on disk
 * and used to keep rendering. The transcript then showed the same user message
 * twice (once at its old position, above output it had already been rewound
 * past) and interleaved the discarded answers with the new ones.
 *
 * Recovery records the discarded seq range on the worker instead, and readers
 * skip those entries. Nothing is deleted; the raw stream stays intact.
 */

export type SupersededSeqRange = {
  /** First superseded seq, inclusive — the original delivery of the message. */
  from: number;
  /** Last superseded seq, inclusive — the stream tip when the rewind happened. */
  through: number;
};

function isUsableRange(range: SupersededSeqRange) {
  return Number.isFinite(range.from)
    && Number.isFinite(range.through)
    && range.from >= 1
    && range.through >= range.from;
}

export function parseSupersededSeqRanges(value: string | null | undefined): SupersededSeqRange[] {
  if (!value?.trim()) {
    return [];
  }
  let parsed: unknown;
  try {
    parsed = JSON.parse(value);
  } catch {
    return [];
  }
  if (!Array.isArray(parsed)) {
    return [];
  }
  const ranges = parsed.flatMap((entry) => {
    if (typeof entry !== "object" || entry === null) {
      return [];
    }
    const record = entry as { from?: unknown; through?: unknown };
    const range = {
      from: Math.floor(Number(record.from)),
      through: Math.floor(Number(record.through)),
    };
    return isUsableRange(range) ? [range] : [];
  });
  return mergeSupersededSeqRanges(ranges);
}

/** Sort and coalesce overlapping/adjacent ranges so the stored list stays small. */
export function mergeSupersededSeqRanges(ranges: SupersededSeqRange[]): SupersededSeqRange[] {
  const usable = ranges.filter(isUsableRange).sort((left, right) => left.from - right.from);
  const merged: SupersededSeqRange[] = [];
  for (const range of usable) {
    const previous = merged.at(-1);
    if (previous && range.from <= previous.through + 1) {
      previous.through = Math.max(previous.through, range.through);
      continue;
    }
    merged.push({ ...range });
  }
  return merged;
}

export function serializeSupersededSeqRanges(ranges: SupersededSeqRange[]): string | null {
  const merged = mergeSupersededSeqRanges(ranges);
  return merged.length > 0 ? JSON.stringify(merged) : null;
}

export function isSupersededSeq(seq: number | null | undefined, ranges: SupersededSeqRange[]) {
  if (typeof seq !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(seq)) {
    return false;
  }
  return ranges.some((range) => seq >= range.from && seq <= range.through);
}

/** Drop the entries that belong to a discarded branch. */
export function withoutSupersededEntries<T extends { seq?: number | null }>(
  entries: T[],
  ranges: SupersededSeqRange[],
): T[] {
  return ranges.length === 0 ? entries : entries.filter((entry) => !isSupersededSeq(entry.seq, ranges));
}

In the typical case without transcript entries, it returns `directWorkerEntries` unchanged, but if there are entries to merge, it creates a new coalesced array each render. Since the unified worker stream path normally has transcript entries, that new array creation is the expected behavior.

The `coalesceWorkerEntriesById` function does an O(n) coalesce operation with a Map and sort, which for long conversations with hundreds or thousands of entries becomes a meaningful cost per render. This forces Terminal's `activity` to recompute as well, which does even heavier work like flatMap and buildAgentOutputActivity. agent?.supersededSeqRanges. The tricky part is that `supersededSeqRanges` is parsed server-side into a new array each snapshot, so it'll bust the memo on SSE frames even if nothing relevant changed — but that's still better than recomputing on every keystroke, which is the main win.

The cleanest approach is to memoize based on a stable key. I'll stringify the ranges to create a stable dependency, then use that to memoize the ranges themselves, and finally memoize the entries computation on those stable ranges. It's a bit of extra work but the ranges list is tiny so it's cheap.

## Claude thinking · 2026-08-03T17:40:00.247Z

The selector is deliberately filtering out keystroke-related state to prevent unnecessary re-renders on HomeApp, so the typing lag isn't coming from input handling itself. The bottleneck is actually agent output frames monopolizing the main thread, which aligns with what the user observed about slowdowns happening whenever an agent is actively producing output.

Beyond the localStorage churn I've already identified as the main culprit, there's a secondary cost: every SSE frame triggers ConversationMain to re-render, which rebuilds the conversation entries and the Terminal activity state. I should measure whether the `coalesceWorkerEntriesById` function and activity building are genuinely expensive on a realistic conversation size to see if it's worth optimizing.

Even though Terminal will re-render when the parent updates, its internal memoization should prevent the expensive activity calculation from running again.   private getCachedEntries(workerId: string): WorkerEntry[] {
    const cached = this.readEnvelope().workers[workerId];
    if (!cached || !isWorkerEntryArray(cached.entries)) {

    return cached.entries;

## Claude thinking · 2026-08-03T17:43:20.873Z

The state objects are structurally identical but the `entries` array is a different reference, which is why my equality check isn't catching it as the same state. The refresh flow likely goes through a different code path that sets `status: "loading"` before merging, causing the reference to change even though the actual data hasn't.

So each poll cycle triggers two notifications — one when status flips to loading, another when it flips back to loaded — which means two re-renders per poll regardless of whether entries actually changed. That's the real problem, though it's separate from the entries identity issue I fixed. The question is whether I should also prevent the loading state flip for background refreshes, or keep the test narrower and just fix the entries reuse. Let me trace through the refresh path to see what's actually happening.

## Claude thinking · 2026-08-03T17:43:35.808Z

I'm seeing the root cause now—`fetchForward` unconditionally sets status to "loading" then back to "loaded" on every poll cycle, triggering two notifications every 2 seconds regardless of whether data actually changed. This is the exact churn that was already causing the message blinking issue someone tried to patch around.

The fix is to only announce "loading" for initial loads when there are no entries yet, not for background revalidations of already-loaded streams. It's a behavior change with some risk, but it's surgical and there's already a `hasEverLoaded` latch in place downstream. Let me search through the codebase to see who's actually consuming `status === "loading"` to understand the full impact before making this change.

## Claude · 2026-08-03T17:47:35.780Z

Done. Both tracks complete, full suite green.

## The 3 test failures — not product bugs

They're ambient environment leakage, and the culprit is the agent CLI running the suite. `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` are exported into my shell; the tests spread `...process.env` into the runtime they spawn; and `manager.ts:326` deliberately *yields* to a caller-supplied storage dir (same for a caller-supplied model at startup). So the runtime took the yield branch and the tests asserting project-scoped pinning failed — on any developer machine with those set, while passing in CI.

Fixed in `tests/setup.ts`, which already establishes exactly this precedent for `OMNIHARNESS_ROOT` ("Never trust an inherited runner root here"). Scrubbed the storage-location and model-selection vars the runtime branches on. All 93 `tests/server/agent-runtime` tests now pass here with no `env -u` prefix, and no product code changed.

## Perf — measured, and mostly disproved

I checked the claims rather than acting on them, and **most did not survive**:

- *"HomeApp has no selector, so keystrokes re-render everything"* — **false**. `selectHomeAppState` explicitly deletes `command`/`commandCursor`, and both `ComposerContainer` and `ConversationComposer` are already `memo`'d. Someone did this deliberately. Keystrokes don't re-render the tree at all — which confirms the lag is purely main-thread blocking from output frames, exactly as you described it.
- *Server-side SSE floor* — unnecessary; after the earlier fix the loop is already throttled by the enriched build.
- *A `updateState` no-op bail* — I wrote it, then couldn't demonstrate it firing on any real path (`getState` bypasses it, `onKnownSeqs` pre-guards, `applyFetchResult` always transitions `loading`→`loaded`). I removed it rather than ship an unproven branch with a bespoke equality function.

Two things were real, with numbers:

1. **`conversationEntries` rebuilt every render** (`ConversationMain.tsx:895`, no `useMemo`), handing `Terminal` a fresh `entries` prop and busting its internal activity memo. Measured **~3.3ms wasted per SSE frame** at 2250 entries on this desktop — several times that on a phone. Now memoized, with `supersededSeqRanges` stabilized because the server re-parses it into a new array every frame and would otherwise bust the memo anyway.
2. **`WorkerEntriesManager` allocated a new `entries` array on every poll** even when nothing was appended (`const merged = [...previous.entries]`), which would have defeated that memo regardless. Now reuses the previous reference. Verified the test fails without it.

Two caveats I want to be straight about. My first activity benchmark was **wrong** — I passed an array where the function wants a snapshot object, got 0 items and a meaningless 0.00ms; the numbers above are from the corrected version. And the cache benchmark used an in-memory stand-in for `localStorage`, so it captures only the JSON work (~3.9ms/update), not the synchronous disk I/O that's the larger term on mobile.

One lifecycle test (`process-session-restart`) flaked once under full-suite parallel load; it passes in isolation and the full suite came back clean on re-run — **374 files, 2428 passed**.
